{{Short description|Type of logical contradiction}}
The '''paradoxes of material implication''' are a group of [[Classical logic|classically]] [[tautology (logic)|true formulae]] involving [[material conditional]]s whose translations into natural language are intuitively [[False statement|false]] when the conditional is translated with English words such as "implies" or "if ... then ...". They are sometimes phrased as ''[[argument]]s'', since they are easily turned into arguments with [[modus ponens]]: if it is true that "if <math> P </math> then <math> Q </math>" (<math> P \rightarrow Q </math>), then from that together with <math> P </math>, one may argue for <math> Q </math>. Among them are the following:

For instance, this proposition is considered classically true: "If [[The Moon is made of green cheese|The moon is made of green cheese]], either it is [[rain]]ing in [[Ecuador]] now or it is not."<ref name=":0" /> So is this one: "If my [[dog]] barks at [[Waste collector|rubbish collectors]], then either it is raining in [[Bolivia]] right now or it is not."<ref name=":1" />

|<math> \lnot p \rightarrow (p \rightarrow q) </math><ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /><ref name=":6" />
|"If it is not the case that P, then if P, then Q"; a false proposition implies any other.<ref name="BunninYu" /> For instance, if [[Socrates]] was not a [[Solar myths|solar myth]], then "Socrates was a solar myth" implies [[2 + 2 = 5|2+2=5]].<ref name=":1" /> Or, given that the moon is not made of cheese, then it is true that "if the moon is made of cheese, it is made of [[ketchup]]".<ref>{{Cite book |last=Blackburn |first=Simon |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=5wTQtwB1NdgC |title=The Oxford Dictionary of Philosophy |date=2005-10-27 |publisher=Oxford University Press, UK |isbn=978-0-19-861013-7 |pages=225 |language=en}}</ref>
|[[vacuous truth]]

G. |date=2014-01-26 |publisher=Princeton University Press |isbn=978-0-691-16044-3 |pages=239 |language=en}}</ref>
|"If it is the case that P and it is not the case that P, then it is the case that Q"; anything follows from a contradiction. For instance, it is a valid argument that "If Pat is both a [[mother]] and not a mother, then Pat is a [[father]]".<ref name=":3">{{Cite book |last=Clark |first=Michael |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=XCMxIZH69EgC |title=Paradoxes from A to Z |date=2012 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-53857-2 |pages=61 |language=en}}</ref>
|[[principle of explosion]], or ''paradox of entailment.''<ref name=":3" /><ref name="cs.utexas.edu">{{Cite book |last1=Rich |first1=Elaine |url=https://www.cs.utexas.edu/~dnp/frege/paradoxes-of-material-implication.html |title="Paradoxes" of Material Implication |last2=Cline |first2=Alan Kaylor |language=en-US}}</ref> It is also a paradox of strict implication.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":4" />
|-
|<math> (p \rightarrow q) \lor (q \rightarrow r) </math><ref name=":0" /><ref name="cs.utexas.edu"/>
|"Either if P then Q, or if Q then R, or both"; a proposition is either implied by any other (which happens when it is true) or implies any other (which happens when it is false). For example, it is a tautologically true proposition that "either the fact that this article was edited by a [[Brazilians|Brazilian]] implies that it is accurate, or this article's accuracy implies that it was edited by an [[English people|Englishman]]".
|No common names in the literature.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" />
|-
|<math> (p \rightarrow q) \lor (q \rightarrow p) </math><ref name=":1" />
|"Either if P then Q, or if Q then P, or both" (a particular case of the above); of two propositions, either the first implies the second, or the second implies the first. For example, it is a tautologically true proposition that "either the [[Continuum hypothesis|Continuum Hypothesis]] implies the [[Collatz conjecture|Collatz Conjecture]], or the Collatz Conjecture implies the Continuum Hypothesis".
|No common names in the literature.<ref name=":1" />
|}
{{Quote box
| quote = [[Bertrand Russell|Russell]]'s definition of "p implies q" as synonymous with "either not p or q" solicited the justified objection that according to it a true proposition is implied by any proposition and a false proposition implies any proposition (paradoxes of material implication).
| author = Arthur Pap
| source = ''Elements of Analytic Philosophy''<ref name="BunninYu" /><ref>{{Cite book |last=Pap |first=Arthur |url=http://archive.org/details/elementsofanalyt0000arth_c2b9 |title=elements of analytic philosophy |date=1949 |publisher=the macmillan company, new york |others=Internet Archive |pages=463}}</ref>

A material conditional formula <math> P \rightarrow Q </math> is true unless <math>P</math> is true and <math>Q</math> is false; it is synonymous with "either P is false, or Q is true, or both". This gives rise to [[vacuous truth]]s such as, "if [[2 + 2 = 5|2+2=5]], then this Wikipedia article is accurate", which is true regardless of the contents of this article, because the [[Antecedent (logic)|antecedent]] is false. Given that such problematic consequences follow from an extremely popular and widely accepted model of reasoning, namely the material implication in [[classical logic]], they are called ''[[paradoxes]]''. They demonstrate a mismatch between classical logic and robust intuitions about [[meaning (philosophy)|meaning]] and [[reasoning]].<ref>{{cite encyclopedia |year=2011 |title=Conditionals |encyclopedia=Semantics: An international handbook of meaning |publisher=de Gruyter Mouton |url=http://mit.edu/fintel/fintel-2011-hsk-conditionals.pdf |last=von Fintel |first=Kai |editor-last1=von Heusinger |editor-first1=Klaus |pages=1515–1538 |doi=10.1515/9783110255072.1515 |isbn=978-3-11-018523-2 |editor-last2=Maienborn |editor-first2=Claudia |editor-first3=Paul |editor-last3=Portner |hdl=1721.1/95781 |hdl-access=free}}</ref>

== Subjunctives (counterfactuals) ==
Another counterintuitive feature of material conditionals which is often discussed in connection with the paradoxes of material implication is that they are unsuited for modelling intuitive reasoning with subjunctive statements.<ref name=":2">{{Cite book |last=Priest |first=Graham |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Gm82ItOO9C4C |title=An Introduction to Non-Classical Logic |date=2001-02-22 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0-521-79434-3 |pages=11–12 |language=en}}</ref> A popular example to illustrate this (so popular that it is used by every source cited in this paragraph) is the '''Oswald–Kennedy example''', due to a 1970 paper by Ernest W. Adams.<ref>{{cite book |last=Lewis |first=David |title=Counterfactuals |date=1973 |publisher=Harvard University Press |isbn=9780631224952 |location=Cambridge, MA |pages=3}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Freudenthal |first=Hans |date=Sep 1975 |title=Ernest W. Adams. Subjunctive and indicative conditionals. Foundations of language, vol. 6 (1970), pp. 89–94. |url=https://doi.org/10.2307/2272204 |journal=Journal of Symbolic Logic |volume=40 |issue=3 |pages=466 |doi=10.2307/2272204 |jstor=2272204 |issn=0022-4812|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name=":1" /> According to Adams, this indicative conditional is true: "If [[Lee Harvey Oswald|Oswald]] did not shoot [[John F. Kennedy|Kennedy]], then someone else did". This is true because [[Assassination of John F. Kennedy|Kennedy was indeed shot]].<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Moreland |first1=J. P. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=mPEN_EDiZuQC |title=Philosophical Foundations for a Christian Worldview |last2=Craig |first2=William Lane |date=2003-03-31 |publisher=InterVarsity Press |isbn=978-0-8308-2694-0 |pages=52 |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":1" /> However, it is generally believed that this subjunctive conditional is not known to be true: "If Oswald hadn't shot Kennedy, someone else would have".<ref>{{Cite book |last=Sider |first=Theodore |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=GK8SEAAAQBAJ |title=Logic for Philosophy |date=2010-01-07 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-265881-4 |pages=200 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Smith |first=Peter |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=udELAQAAQBAJ |title=An Introduction to Formal Logic |date=2003-11-06 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-1-107-49458-9 |pages=137 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=MacFarlane |first=John |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=RaEGEAAAQBAJ |title=Philosophical Logic: A Contemporary Introduction |date=2020-11-29 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-351-73356-4 |pages=97 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Jacquette |first=Dale |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=pzf7_sT58PUC |title=A Companion to Philosophical Logic |date=2008-04-15 |publisher=John Wiley & Sons |isbn=978-1-4051-4994-5 |pages=58 |language=en}}</ref> (Many sources reserve the name of "counterfactual conditional" for the subjunctive,<ref>{{Cite book |last=Gibbard |first=Allan |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Dclz4uKmdCgC |title=Meaning and Normativity |date=2012-12-13 |publisher=OUP Oxford |isbn=978-0-19-964607-4 |pages=133 |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":1" /> although if Oswald did shoot Kennedy, both conditionals are ''counterfactual'' in the sense of having an antecedent which is "contrary to fact", which is still a current usage, although less popular.)<ref>{{Citation |last=Starr |first=Willow |title=Counterfactuals |date=2022 |encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |editor-last=Zalta |editor-first=Edward N. |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/win2022/entries/counterfactuals/ |access-date=2025-07-24 |edition=Winter 2022 |publisher=Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University |editor2-last=Nodelman |editor2-first=Uri}}</ref> Even if someone believes himself to know the truth of the subjunctive conditional, he would still usually think that it has a different meaning or content from the indicative conditional.<ref name=":2" /> However, if someone were to model both using the material conditional in propositional logic, they would both be <math> \lnot O \rightarrow S </math>, read "if it is not the case that O, then it is the case that S", where O stands for "Oswald shot Kennedy" and S stands for "Someone else shot Kennedy". This modelling, if accepted for both statements, would imply that the indicative and the subjunctive statement are equivalent, which is counterintuitive and thus, in this sense, paradoxical. Given such a model, a supporter of the [[Nazi Party]] could validly argue in classical logic, for instance, that "If the [[Nazism|Nazis]] had won [[World War II|World War Two]], everybody would be happy", which is [[vacuously true]] because it is indeed false that the Nazis won World War Two.

{{Quote box
| quote = If we extend [[Material conditional|this convention]] to human activities, then the statement "If [[Adolf Hitler|Hitler]] had won World War II then [[European integration|Europe would now be a single nation]]" is [[Vacuous truth|trivially true]], because [[Aftermath of World War II|Hitler did not win World War II]]. But "If Hitler had won World War II then [[When pigs fly|pigs would now have wings]]" is also trivially true, for the same reason. In [[modal logic]], however, it would be sensible to debate the truth or falsity of the first of these statements, depending on how [[history]] might have changed if the Nazis had won the war. The second would be false, because [[pig]]s don't have [[wings]].
| author = [[Ian Stewart (mathematician)|Ian Stewart]]
| source = ''Professor Stewart's Cabinet of Mathematical Curiosities''<ref>{{Cite book |last=Stewart |first=Ian |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=tPt0xwqeLSAC |title=Professor Stewart's Cabinet of Mathematical Curiosities |date=2009-01-06 |publisher=Basic Books |isbn=978-0-7867-2725-4 |pages=248 |language=en}}</ref>
| width = 30%
| align = right
}}

Although examples such as the Oswald–Kennedy example are widely seen as motivating an analysis of subjunctives which is different from the material conditional, theorists (philosophers, logicians, semanticists) differ on precisely what analysis of subjunctives to use in place of the material conditional. Some analyze subjunctive conditionals as fundamentally different from indicative,<ref name=":5">{{Cite book |last=Khoo |first=Justin |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=eJtlEAAAQBAJ |title=The Meaning of If |date=2022 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-009670-0 |pages=51–53 |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":1" /> some instead view all conditionals as having a domain or context,<ref name=":5" /> and some analyses focus on accounting for verb tense, viewing the distinctive feature of these conditionals as that they have an antecedent which is in the past.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Gabbay |first1=Dov M. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=IoTtCAAAQBAJ |title=Handbook of Philosophical Logic: Volume II: Extensions of Classical Logic |last2=Guenthner |first2=Franz |date=2012-12-06 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-94-009-6259-0 |pages=140 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Girle |first=Rod |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=XqHCBQAAQBAJ |title=Modal Logics and Philosophy |date=2014-12-05 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-317-49217-7 |pages=224–225 |language=en}}</ref>

== Solutions ==
Classical logic, with the material implication connective, remains widely used despite the paradoxes, because most users simply get used to them or ignore them, judging the paradoxes to be minor drawbacks compared with the benefits of the material conditional's "considerable virtues of simplicity"<ref name=":8">{{Citation |last1=Egré |first1=Paul |title=The Logic of Conditionals |date=2021 |encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |editor-last=Zalta |editor-first=Edward N. |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/win2021/entries/logic-conditionals/ |access-date=2025-07-24 |edition=Winter 2021 |publisher=Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University |last2=Rott |first2=Hans}}</ref> and [[Strength (mathematical logic)|logical strength]].<ref name=":8" /> [[Alan Ross Anderson|Anderson]] and [[Nuel Belnap|Belnap]], in their seminal book ''Entailment'' on [[Relevance logic|relevant logic]], represented what they called the "Official" (classical-logical) view as follows:<blockquote>
To be sure, there are certain odd theorems such as A→(B→A) and A→(B→B) which might offend the naive, and indeed these have been referred to in the literature as "paradoxes of implication." But this terminology reflects a misunderstanding. "If A, then if B then A" really means no more than "Either not-A, or else not-B or A," and the latter is clearly a [[logical truth]]; hence so is the former. Properly understood there are no "paradoxes" of implication.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Anderson |first1=Alan Ross |title=Entailment: The Logic of Relevance and Neccessity, Vol. I |last2=Belnap |first2=Nuel D. |date=1975 |publisher=Princeton University Press |pages=3}}</ref></blockquote>
Similarly, [[E. J. Lemmon|E.J. Lemmon]] was conscious of the suspicious appearance of the paradoxes, and designed his popular textbook ''Beginning Logic'' to subtly discourage suspicion about them, by first introducing the [[natural deduction]] rules for [[propositional logic]] and only speaking of [[truth table]]s afterwards.<ref name="LemmonLogic">{{Cite book |last=Lemmon |first=E. J. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=qkmG04_ecLMC |title=Beginning Logic |date=1971-09-30 |publisher=CRC Press |isbn=978-0-412-38090-7 |pages=ix |language=en |quote=Any student worth his salt is going to be suspicious of the paradoxes of material implication. This fact counts strongly against beginning the treatment of the propositional calculus with the truth-table method. Accordingly, I have tried to woo the student in Chapter 1 into acceptance of a set of rules from which the paradoxes flow as natural consequences in Chapter 2; the truth-table method is then partly justified by appeal to these rules. Any teacher, therefore, who thinks that the paradoxes present real problems will (rightly) find my tactics underhand.}}</ref>

=== Strict implication ===
{{Main|Strict conditional}}
[[C. I. Lewis|C.I. Lewis]] was motivated by the paradoxes <math> \lnot p \rightarrow (p \rightarrow q) </math> and <math> p \rightarrow (q \rightarrow p) </math> to invent [[Strict conditional|strict implication]].<ref name=":7">{{Citation |last=Ballarin |first=Roberta |title=Modern Origins of Modal Logic |date=2023 |encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |editor-last=Zalta |editor-first=Edward N. |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/fall2023/entries/logic-modal-origins/ |access-date=2025-07-24 |edition=Fall 2023 |publisher=Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University |editor2-last=Nodelman |editor2-first=Uri}}</ref> Strict implication retains the [[principle of explosion]] <math> (p \land \lnot p) \rightarrow q </math>, which Lewis regarded as an [[A priori and a posteriori|a priori truth]], but which others still consider a paradox (a "paradox of strict implication") since an impossibility such as 2+2=5 can seem ''irrelevant'' to various facts which one may try to prove from it.<ref name=":7" />

=== Relevance logic ===
{{Main|Relevance logic}}
The paradoxes of material and strict implication have been motivations for the development of [[relevance logic]]s (also called ''relevant logics''), where the principles of logic are weakened in ways that prevent the derivation of the paradoxes as valid.<ref name=":0" />
